Content:
Any multiplication of fractions can also be interpreted as multiplication and division of whole numbers.

Content:
For example, consider

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{14}{\color{blue}3} \times \dfrac{6}{\color{red}7}.]

Content:
Writing the fractions as division, our expression becomes
[MATH: (14\,{\color{blue}{\div\, 3}})\times (6\,{\color{red}{\div\, 7}}) .]
We use parentheses to make it easier to read.

Content:
Since our expression contains multiplication and division only, we can write an equivalent expression by swapping the two divisions. Swapping the [MATH: {\color{red}{\div\, 3}}] and the [MATH: {\color{blue}{\div\, 7}}], we get the following equivalent expression:
[MATH: (14\, {\color{red}{\div\, 7}}) \times (6\, {\color{blue}{\div\, 3}})]

Content:
If we interpret the divisions as fractions again, then we have another equivalent expression:
[MATH: \dfrac{14}{\color{red}7} \times \dfrac{6}{\color{blue}3}]

Content:
Notice that this amounts to swapping the denominators in the original expression.

items.readable_text:
Content:
When solving a fraction multiplication problem, it's often convenient to simplify the problem before carrying out the multiplication.

Content:
For example, let's consider the following multiplication problem:

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{\color{red}3}{8} \times \dfrac{1}{\color{blue}12}]

Content:
Notice that the first fraction's numerator ([MATH: \color{red}3]) and the second fraction's denominator ([MATH: \color{blue}12]) have a common
factor of [MATH: 3.]

Content:
Therefore, we can simplify our problem by first swapping the denominators:

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{\color{red}3}{\color{blue}12} \times \dfrac{1}{8}]

Content:
Next, we reduce the first fraction to its lowest terms by dividing the numerator and denominator by [MATH: 3.]

Content:
[MATH: (3 ÷ 3)/(12 ÷ 3) × (1)/(8)|= (1)/(4) × (1)/(8)]

Content:
To multiply two fractions, we multiply the numerators and we multiply the denominators:

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{1}{4} \times \dfrac{1}{8} = \dfrac{1 \times 1}{4 \times 8} = \dfrac{1}{32}]

Content:
Therefore, we conclude that

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{3}{8} \times \dfrac{1}{12} = \dfrac{1}{32}.]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Any multiplication of fractions can also be interpreted as multiplication and division of whole numbers.

Content:
For example, consider

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{14}{\color{blue}3} \times \dfrac{6}{\color{red}7}.]

Content:
Writing the fractions as division, our expression becomes
[MATH: (14\,{\color{blue}{\div\, 3}})\times (6\,{\color{red}{\div\, 7}}) .]
We use parentheses to make it easier to read.

Content:
Since our expression contains multiplication and division only, we can write an equivalent expression by swapping the two divisions. Swapping the [MATH: {\color{red}{\div\, 3}}] and the [MATH: {\color{blue}{\div\, 7}}], we get the following equivalent expression:
[MATH: (14\, {\color{red}{\div\, 7}}) \times (6\, {\color{blue}{\div\, 3}})]

Content:
If we interpret the divisions as fractions again, then we have another equivalent expression:
[MATH: \dfrac{14}{\color{red}7} \times \dfrac{6}{\color{blue}3}]

Content:
Notice that this amounts to swapping the denominators in the original expression.

---

The given expression is

Since our expression contains multiplication and division only, we can write an equivalent expression by swapping the [MATH: {\color{red}{\div\, 5}}] and the [MATH: {\color{blue}{\div\, 13}}]:
[MATH: (15\, {\color{red}{\div\, 5}}) \times (4\, {\color{blue}{\div\, 13}})]

We can now interpret the divisions as fractions:
[MATH: \dfrac{15} 5 \times \dfrac 4 {13}]

So the missing fraction is [MATH: \dfrac{15} 5.]
